paper_a.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning (Mnih et al., 2013)

paper_b.title: Neural Fitted Q Iteration - First Experiences with a Data Efficient Neural Reinforcement Learning Method (Riedmiller, 2005)

metadata.description: DQN extends Neural Fitted Q Iteration by: (1) using deep convolutional networks processing raw pixel inputs (vs. hand-crafted state features), (2) online learning with experience replay (vs. batch learning from a fixed dataset), (3) target network for stability, and (4) scaling to high-dimensional Atari environments. The core idea -- using a neural network to approximate Q-values from stored transitions -- is shared.

matches.explanation: Both define Q-learning with function approximation targeting the Bellman equation $Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a')]$. The mathematical framework is identical: learn $Q$ by minimizing TD error over collected transitions.

Both use neural networks to approximate Q-values, but with very different architectures. NFQ: small MLP (2-3 hidden layers, 20-50 units) taking (state, action) pair as input, outputting one Q-value. DQN: deep convolutional network taking raw pixels as input, outputting Q-values for all actions simultaneously. DQN's architecture enables learning from high-dimensional sensory input.

Both reuse stored transitions for learning. NFQ: collect all experiences into a fixed batch $\mathcal{D}$, then do multiple full passes (fitted Q iterations). DQN: continuously add new experiences to a replay buffer and sample random minibatches for online SGD updates. DQN's experience replay is an online adaptation of NFQ's batch paradigm.

Both iterate: compute Q-targets from current network, train network on these targets. NFQ: retrain entire network from scratch each iteration. DQN: continuously update via SGD on minibatches, with a separate target network updated periodically. DQN's approach is more scalable but less stable without the target network.

Both discuss the benefits of learning from stored transitions. NFQ: batch learning enables data efficiency and multiple passes. DQN: experience replay provides decorrelation, data reuse, and stability. Same underlying insight that reusing transitions improves learning.
DQN's frame preprocessing (grayscale conversion, stacking 4 frames, reward clipping) is specific to the Atari visual domain and has no NFQ counterpart.
Epsilon-greedy with annealing over 1M frames is DQN-specific. NFQ uses a fixed exploration strategy appropriate for its batch setting.

Both demonstrate successful learning on control tasks. NFQ: cart-pole swing-up from ~100 episodes. DQN: superhuman Atari play from raw pixels. DQN operates at a fundamentally different scale (high-dimensional observations, long horizons, complex dynamics).
